chunks: Testing ICs at board level. The question: How do you test ICs at the board-level?
Testing a chip on a finished board means proving three things in order: it has what it needs to run, it can talk, and it does its job.
You go from cheap, safe checks to deeper ones, because a healthy chip in a bad setting looks dead.
Think of a car that will not start. You check the fuel, the battery and the key, then listen for the starter, and only then suspect the engine.
A chip works the same way: without power, or held stopped, or with no ticking signal, it stays silent even though it is fine.
One gap: you cannot see inside a chip, so you question it through its pins.
Each rung assumes the one above passed. If the ID read fails, return to the first two rungs before suspecting the IC.
Supply: the voltage the chip is powered from, measured at the chip's own pins. Reset: a pin that holds the chip stopped until it is released.
Clock: a steady ticking signal that paces everything the chip does. ID register: a fixed number stored in the chip that it reports when asked, such as a WHO AM I value.
I2C and SPI: two common short links a processor uses to read and write a chip's registers. Known-good board: a working copy of the board you compare against.
A sensor chip runs from a 3. 3 volts supply line (a "rail"). First, put a meter on the chip's own supply pin: anything from 3. 20 volts to 3. 40 volts is fine.
Check that reset is released and the clock is ticking. Then ask the chip for its ID register over I2C.
If it returns the number the datasheet promises, the chip is powered, soldered correctly and talking.
If the read fails or comes back as all ones (0xFF), nobody answered, so go back to supply, reset and clock before blaming the chip. That is the whole idea.

"I use a ladder: confirm supply, ground, reset, clock and strap pins at the IC; check supply current and temperature; use diode-mode checks on pins for a damage signature; read the ID register over I2C or SPI; use JTAG boundary scan where available; program and read back or run self-tests; and compare with a known-good board.
A successful ID read proves the part and its solder joints work in the circuit."
